name: The Nation cryptic crossword No 3501
preamble: Puzzled? No more cross words! Read Kosman and Picciotto on “Solving The Nation’s Cryptic Puzzles.” Or watch this video.

clue.text: At first, acute pressure to back up claims

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening letter of the next word only
to back up is to move backwards, so the word read this way runs from its end

blocks.note: the first letter of acute
stress is pressure or strain

explanation.surface: A sharp burst of pressure at the start helps to support someone's claims.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert something is to state it firmly as true, which is exactly what claiming it means.

clue.text: Keep reusing garment materials as a way to stay cool

indicators.note: reusing material means remaking it into something new, and here some of it is used twice over

blocks.note: the letters of garment, with its E and N used a second time
to keep something going is to manage it, as in keeping house

explanation.surface: Recycling the fabric of your clothes, offered as a tip for keeping cool in summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stay cool' suggests beating the heat but means keeping your temper. 'Reusing' is literal: garment's E and N are each used twice, and the word for keep sits inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger management is therapy for controlling one's temper, a way of keeping calm rather than flaring up.

clue.text: Legal actions of executives

blocks.note: first meaning: lawsuits brought in court
second meaning: slang for business executives, from their formal clothes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests lawsuits filed by company bosses; the two meanings belong to one plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawsuits are the court cases people file, and office slang calls managers by the business attire they wear.

clue.text: Urchin runs over to conceal error

indicators.note: concealing something means hiding it within, so one piece is tucked inside another

blocks.note: R is the cricket and baseball scoring abbreviation for runs
to do something over is to do it again
a muff is a fumbled catch or blunder

explanation.surface: A street kid runs back to cover up a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' here means once more, as in American 'do it over', not finished or across.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragamuffin is a ragged, dirty child of the streets, the same figure as an urchin.

clue.text: Second piece of furniture is not likely to fall

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
a table is a piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A second-hand piece of furniture that at least won't topple over.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stable is steady and firmly balanced, so it is unlikely to tip or collapse.

clue.text: Like one receiving a pension or new wheels?

definitions.note: read with 'Like one receiving': describing a car given fresh tyres

blocks.note: first meaning: having stopped working for good
second meaning: fitted with tires again

explanation.surface: A playful question: what do a pensioner and a car fresh from the garage have in common?
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a pun: read it as RE-TIRED, given new tires (tyres in British spelling).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone drawing a pension has usually left work for good, which is the ordinary sense of being retired.

clue.text: Brooks and birds, running

blocks.note: robins are birds
a machine that is running is on

explanation.surface: Streams and birds both running along, a country scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brooks' looks like streams, but it is a first name: Brooks Robinson was a famous US baseball third baseman for the Baltimore Orioles.
explanation.definitionFit: A first name can clue a surname when one famous person owns it, as the baseball great Brooks Robinson does.

clue.text: Bishop's skirt

blocks.note: first meaning: Desmond ..., the South African archbishop
second meaning: a ballerina's short stiff skirt

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests a bishop's vestment; the 's stands for 'is', joining two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Archbishop Desmond Tutu was the famous anti-apartheid churchman, and a ballet dancer's frilled skirt has the same name.

clue.text: Applaud Panama, say, for invasive operation

blocks.note: to root for a team is to cheer or applaud it
the Panama is an example of a canal, as 'say' signals

explanation.surface: Cheering Panama on as it faces an invasion, a political headline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panama' suggests the country or the hat; 'say' marks it as an example of a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: A root canal is dental surgery drilling into the tooth's pulp, a genuinely invasive procedure.

clue.text: Confused, having expanded outside small band at second-rate university

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps around the rest

blocks.note: dilated means widened or expanded
S is the abbreviation for small
a combo is a small jazz band
B grade is second-rate
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A small band playing at a mediocre college has grown too big and is now thoroughly mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Discombobulated is a jokey American word for disconcerted, flustered or bewildered, all ways of being confused.

clue.text: En route, I smuggled in bell

indicators.note: something smuggled in is slipped secretly inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: a gong is a bell-like instrument that is struck
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller confesses to sneaking a bell through customs while on the way somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is going somewhere is on the way there, the meaning of the borrowed French phrase en route.

clue.text: Enterprising stratagem after disposing of initial debts

indicators.note: getting rid of the initial means the opening letter of the word is dropped
one thing placed after another fixes the order, so the second piece comes second

blocks.note: a gambit is an opening ploy or stratagem
IOUs are written promises to repay debts

explanation.surface: An enterprising plan for getting out of debt, read as a business pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as if the stratagem disposes of debts, but 'disposing of initial' acts on the stratagem's own first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An enterprising person shows drive and eagerness to achieve, which is what ambitious describes.

clue.text: Like a bit of sapphire amid mere counterfeit jewelry

indicators.note: just a bit of the next word means only its first letter is used
a counterfeit is a fake made up to look different, so these letters are rearranged
something amid other things sits in their middle, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the first letter of sapphire
taken as written, to be rearranged
bling is slang for flashy jewelry

explanation.surface: A chip of genuine sapphire sits among a pile of fake jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like the start of a description, but it is the definition; a bit of sapphire goes inside MERE rearranged as REEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying one thing is like another means it resembles it, so the preposition matches the participle in use.

clue.text: Computer person losing head with love, love, love…

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

blocks.note: a tech is a computer technician
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A tech worker who has lost their head over love, repeating the word endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'love' supplies a letter; the fading 'love, love…' after it is the definition, a word coming back fainter each time.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo is a sound repeated back more and more faintly, exactly as the trailing repetitions on the page suggest.

clue.text: Garden tool interfering with plant disease is a safety feature

indicators.note: something interfering with another gets in among it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: blight is a plant disease
a rake is a garden tool

explanation.surface: A gardener's tool meddling with diseased plants is meant as a precaution.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake light glows when a car slows, warning drivers behind, so it is a vehicle safety device.

clue.text: Commercial break without purpose

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial
a rift is a break or split

explanation.surface: A TV commercial break that seems to serve no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial break' reads as one phrase, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A drifting boat has no direction, so adrift figuratively means aimless, lacking any purpose.

clue.text: Hopper looks for oil and gas — they're on top of the car

definitions.text: they're on top of the car

blocks.note: a roo, short for kangaroo, is a hopper
fracking is drilling and fracturing rock to extract oil and gas

explanation.surface: A road-trip scene: someone searches for fuel while the luggage rides on the car roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hopper' suggests Edward Hopper or a grain hopper; it is the kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: Roof racks are frames fixed above a car for carrying luggage or bikes, so they sit on top of the car.

clue.text: Nerd goes around globe with no better than average means of access

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a dork is a nerd
a globe is round, like the letter O
taken as written
a B grade is one step better than an average C

explanation.surface: A nerd travels the world with only mediocre means of getting in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no better than average' reads as one phrase, but it splits as 'no' and 'better than average', the B grade.
explanation.definitionFit: You turn a doorknob to open a door, so it is quite literally how you get access to a room.

clue.text: Blue law inscribed in broken cane

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters are put back in a new order
inscribed in means written inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a rule is a law

explanation.surface: A puritanical law carved into a snapped walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue law' reads as one phrase, an American Sunday-closing law, but 'Blue' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerulean is a deep sky-blue colour, so it is a shade of blue.

clue.text: Perfume dispenser talking at a cheapskate

indicators.note: talking means the following words are judged by how they are spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a miser is a cheapskate, and the phrase said quickly gives the word

explanation.surface: Someone spraying perfume while talking at a stingy companion.
explanation.walkthrough: A miser is a cheapskate; say 'at a miser' quickly and it runs together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An atomizer turns liquid into a fine spray, the device on a scent bottle that dispenses perfume.

clue.text: Flat stone housing Kentucky research facility

indicators.note: housing something means holding it inside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a slab is a flat piece of stone
KY is the postal abbreviation for Kentucky

explanation.surface: A stone slab being used to house a research lab in Kentucky.
explanation.walkthrough: Skylab was the first US space station, in orbit in the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: Skylab was an orbiting laboratory where astronauts ran experiments, so it was a research facility in space.

clue.text: Feverish, except for the face (it is an ailment)

indicators.note: the face of a word is its front, so everything but its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: feverish means hot
taken as written

explanation.surface: A feverish patient whose face alone is spared, with a doctor's aside naming the illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket hides the letters: 'it is' run together is the medical suffix for inflammation.
explanation.definitionFit: Otitis is inflammation of the ear, a medical condition and so an ailment.

clue.text: What you need to think without limits: money

indicators.note: with its limits gone, the word loses its letters at both ends

blocks.note: a neuron is a nerve cell, the unit the brain thinks with

explanation.surface: A self-help maxim: to think without limits, all you need is money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'think without limits' reads as a motivational phrase, but 'without limits' trims the brain cell at both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the currency of most of the European Union, so it is a kind of money.

clue.text: Written right to left in Avignon, the calfskin describes that object with many stories

indicators.note: to describe in the geometric sense is to draw around, so one piece goes around another
writing from right to left runs the letters backwards, as Hebrew or Arabic does

blocks.note: Avignon is a French city, and in French 'the' is le
vellum is fine parchment made from calfskin
it is the pronoun for that object

explanation.surface: A French manuscript on calfskin, written right to left, describes a many-storied tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stories' suggests tales, but in the definition it means floors (storeys in British spelling) of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A building with many stories has many floors, so it is a multilevel structure, as a car park might be.

clue.text: Old-fashioned recording, like "Jungle Love" at the beginning

indicators.note: only what is at the beginning counts, so just the word's opening letter is used

blocks.note: a jungle is full of vines, so jungle-like is viny
the first letter of Love

explanation.surface: An old record of the song Jungle Love, heard right at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: "Jungle Love" in quotes looks like one song title, but it splits: 'like Jungle' gives the adjective and 'Love' only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinyl records are the old pre-digital format for music, so vinyl is a retro recording medium.

clue.text: Beat of young reporter including legislature's opening

indicators.note: an opening is the first part, so only the word's first letter is taken
including something means holding it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a cub reporter is a young, inexperienced journalist
the first letter of legislature

explanation.surface: A junior journalist covering the legislature's opening as their beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a reporter's patch, but here it is a verb meaning to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: To club someone is to hit them with a heavy stick, so it means to beat.

clue.text: Sound arrangement of skeleton is outstanding

indicators.note: sound tells the solver to say the letters out loud and listen to the word they make

blocks.note: a skeleton arrangement is a bare-bones spelling, four letters standing for a whole word as in text-speak

explanation.surface: A judge praises how a skeleton has been put together, perhaps in a museum display.
explanation.walkthrough: The skeleton is the text-speak spelling XLNT; read those four letter names aloud, ex-el-en-tee, and you hear the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something excellent is of the very highest quality, so it stands out from the rest.

clue.text: Man takes in Eastern playwright

indicators.note: taking something in means admitting it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a gent is a gentleman, a man
E is the abbreviation for Eastern

explanation.surface: A man takes in the work of a playwright from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Genet was a French novelist and playwright, author of The Maids and The Balcony.
explanation.definitionFit: Genet wrote stage plays such as The Balcony, so he is an example of a playwright.

clue.text: Spooner's optimal skin tone is the subject of a treaty

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the next phrase is treated likewise

blocks.note: optimal is best and a skin tone from the sun is a tan; swap their first sounds

explanation.surface: The perfect suntan, absurdly, becomes the matter of an international treaty.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the B and T sounds of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A test ban forbids nuclear weapons testing, the subject of treaties such as the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

clue.text: Certain back muscles captivating alien

indicators.note: going back means the word is read from its end towards its start
to captivate is literally to take captive, so one piece holds the other inside

blocks.note: delts are the deltoid muscles of the shoulder
ET is the film's extraterrestrial, an alien

explanation.surface: Some back muscles prove irresistible to a visiting alien.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back muscles' reads as one phrase, the lats, but 'back' is an instruction acting on 'muscles'.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter that is settled is decided beyond doubt, so it is certain.
